title: 2 Corinthians 13:5–10
context: Paul turns the Corinthians’ demand for proof of his ministry into an invitation to examine their own faith and recognise Christ’s presence among them. His prayer is for their good conduct and restoration, even if that leaves him appearing weak. The authority he received from the Lord exists to build up the community, so he writes now to avoid a severe confrontation later.

verses.text: Examine your own selves, whether you are in the faith. Test your own selves. Or don’t you know about your own selves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you are disqualified.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul turns their demand to test him back upon them: they must examine whether they are in the faith and recognise Christ among them. Arminian readers stress present trust in Christ and a life responsive to his grace. Many connect this warning with the possibility of abandoning faith, though the verse does not describe a particular person losing salvation. Examination should lead to repentance and renewed assurance, not endless anxiety.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see self-examination as a test of genuine faith, not a denial that believers may know Christ dwells in them. Final unbelief would expose a false profession, while warnings help preserve true believers. Paul also appeals to the congregation’s own experience of Christ as evidence relevant to his ministry. The verse must not be reduced to a demand for flawless conduct as proof of acceptance.
verses.keyContrast: Both call for honest examination grounded in Christ rather than moral perfection or perpetual doubt. Arminian readers commonly connect the warning with the need to continue in faith and the possibility of apostasy; Reformed readers distinguish false profession from saving faith that God preserves. The immediate argument tests the Corinthians’ faith in relation to their challenge to Paul and does not by itself settle the whole perseverance debate.

verses.text: But I hope that you will know that we aren’t disqualified.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul hopes their self-examination will also help them recognise that his ministry has not failed the test. Arminian readers see their faith and his service as related: recognising Christ’s work among them should challenge their rejection of his messenger. The concern is faithful ministry, not a claim that Paul is beyond correction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise connect this hope with the demand for proof in verse 3. Christ’s work through Paul is not invalidated by his unimpressive appearance. Both traditions distinguish approval in this ministerial dispute from speculation about a hidden decree concerning particular individuals.

verses.text: Now I pray to God that you do no evil; not that we may appear approved, but that you may do that which is honorable, though we may seem to have failed.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul prays for their good conduct even if it leaves him looking unsuccessful. Arminian readers stress that divine help and responsible action belong together: he asks God to enable the response he desires. Their restoration matters more than proving his power by exercising discipline.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see dependence on God expressed in prayer for the congregation’s holiness. Paul would rather seem weak than establish his standing through a painful confrontation. Both traditions find a pastoral priority here: the people’s good takes precedence over the minister’s reputation.

verses.text: For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul’s authority serves the truth rather than standing above it. Arminian readers see a limit on every claim to spiritual power: it cannot properly be used to oppose the gospel or protect personal prestige. His hope is that their obedience will make corrective action unnecessary.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise understand apostolic power as commissioned for the truth, not available for arbitrary ends. The statement describes ministry’s allegiance rather than claiming that ministers are incapable of wrongdoing. Both traditions affirm that church authority must be judged by its faithfulness to Christ’s message.

verses.text: For we rejoice when we are weak and you are strong. We also pray for this: your becoming perfect.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul rejoices if their strength allows him to appear weak and prays for their restoration. Arminian readers understand becoming perfect here as being put right and brought to maturity, not a demand for instant flawlessness. Grace is sought in prayer so that the community can respond faithfully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the congregation’s maturity as God’s gift and the goal of pastoral labour. Paul’s apparent weakness is welcome if it means no severe intervention is needed. Both traditions read this prayer in light of the community’s need for repair, rather than treating it as a complete account of Christian perfection.

verses.text: For this cause I write these things while absent, that I may not deal sharply when present, according to the authority which the Lord gave me for building up and not for tearing down.
verses.arminianNotes: The letter aims to secure repentance before the visit, so that sharp correction will not be necessary. Arminian readers stress the opportunity to respond to warning and the constructive purpose of authority. Even severe measures must seek restoration rather than the satisfaction of defeating an opponent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasise authority as a gift from the Lord for building his church. Written warning is itself a pastoral means toward that end. Like Arminian readers, they distinguish necessary correction from destructive leadership that treats people as obstacles to a minister’s success.
